fields.Front: What two independent decisions generate the four dependency patterns?
fields.Back: (1) What type does the class depend on: a concrete class (Paypal) or an abstraction (IPaymentProcessor)? (2) Who creates the collaborator: the class instantiates it itself, or it is injected from outside (usually through the constructor)? Two choices with two options each give four patterns.

fields.Front: Describe pattern 1, Concrete + Instantiate, with its code and verdict.
fields.Back: The class creates and owns a concrete type: class Checkout { Paypal processor; public: void process(double a){ processor.pay(a);} }; and main just writes Checkout c;. Tightest coupling, least flexible: to switch to Stripe or to test without hitting PayPal you must edit Checkout.

fields.Front: Describe pattern 2, Concrete + Inject, with its code and verdict.
fields.Back: class Checkout { Paypal& processor; public: Checkout(Paypal& p) : processor(p) {} ... }; with main writing Paypal paypal; Checkout c(paypal);. Creation has moved out, which is progress, but the parameter type is still Paypal&, so you cannot pass a Stripe processor or a test double.

fields.Front: Describe pattern 3, Abstract + Instantiate, with its code and verdict.
fields.Back: IPaymentProcessor exists and Paypal/Stripe implement it, but Checkout still declares Paypal p1; Stripe p2; by value and calls p1.pay(amount/2); p2.pay(amount/2);. Polymorphism exists in principle but Checkout does not use it, so adding or swapping a processor still means editing Checkout.

fields.Front: Describe pattern 4, Abstract + Inject, with its code and verdict.
fields.Back: class Checkout { IPaymentProcessor& processor; public: Checkout(IPaymentProcessor& p) : processor(p) {} void process(double a){ processor.pay(a);} }; Checkout never names a concrete type. Most flexible (add Crypto : public IPaymentProcessor with no change) and most testable (inject a FakeProcessor).

fields.Front: Why is pattern 3 NOT the Dependency Inversion Principle even though an interface exists?
fields.Back: Checkout still declares Paypal p1; Stripe p2; by value, so it names, creates, and owns the concretes. DIP requires the high-level module to depend ONLY on the abstraction; merely having an interface in the file is not enough.

fields.Front: State the Dependency Inversion Principle using the Checkout example.
fields.Back: High-level modules (Checkout) do not depend on low-level modules (Paypal, Stripe); both depend on an abstraction (IPaymentProcessor). Checkout holds IPaymentProcessor& and the concrete is injected at run time.

fields.Front: Write the IPaymentProcessor interface exactly as it appears in the slides.
fields.Back: class IPaymentProcessor { public: virtual ~IPaymentProcessor() = default; virtual void pay(double amount) = 0; }; A C++ interface is a class containing only pure virtual functions plus a virtual destructor; the I prefix is the course's naming convention.

fields.Front: Why must an interface declare virtual ~IPaymentProcessor() = default;?
fields.Back: A virtual destructor ensures the derived class's destructor runs when an object is deleted through a base-class pointer; without it the derived destructor is skipped and resources leak. = default asks the compiler to generate the ordinary body.

fields.Front: What does Checkout(IPaymentProcessor& p) : processor(p) {} implement, and what is the alternative it replaces?
fields.Back: Constructor injection: the member reference is bound to whatever concrete processor the caller passes. It replaces the class creating its own collaborator internally, which is what made patterns 1 and 3 rigid.

fields.Front: Why is processor.pay(amount) in pattern 4 called a polymorphic call?
fields.Back: pay is virtual and processor is a reference to the base type, so C++ looks up the actual object's type at run time and calls Paypal::pay or Stripe::pay accordingly. Checkout never knows which one it got.

fields.Front: What does pattern 3's Checkout c; c.process(100.0); print, and why?
fields.Back: Paid $50 with Paypal then Paid $50 with Stripe: process splits the amount with p1.pay(amount/2); p2.pay(amount/2); over the two owned concrete members.

fields.Front: State the guiding principle of the coupling-choices lecture and the one-line reason behind it.
fields.Back: Couple to abstractions, not concretions. Dependencies shape flexibility: the type you name in a member declaration is the type you are stuck with.

fields.Text: The four dependency patterns from worst to best: {{c1::Concrete + Instantiate}}, {{c1::Concrete + Inject}}, {{c1::Abstract + Instantiate}}, {{c1::Abstract + Inject}} (DIP).
Summary table: Concrete + Instantiate -> {{c1::Composition}}; Concrete + Inject -> {{c1::Aggregation}}; Abstract + Instantiate -> {{c1::Composition}}; Abstract + Inject -> {{c1::Aggregation}}.
fields.Extra: Instantiate always means composition (the class owns what it creates); inject always means aggregation (the class borrows what it is given).

fields.Text: In C++, composition is a member held {{c1::by value}} (Paypal processor;) and aggregation is a member held {{c1::by reference}} (IPaymentProcessor& processor;) bound in the {{c1::constructor}}.

In pattern 4, Checkout c1(paypal); c1.process(120.0); prints {{c1::Paid $120 with Paypal}} and Checkout c2(stripe); c2.process(80.0); prints {{c1::Paid $80 with Stripe}} - from the {{c1::same}} Checkout class.
A C++ interface is a class containing only {{c1::pure virtual}} functions, declared with {{c1::= 0}}, plus a {{c1::virtual destructor}}; implementations mark their methods with {{c1::override}}.
Concrete + Instantiate is the {{c1::tightest}} coupling and least flexible; Abstract + Inject is the {{c1::most flexible and testable}} and implements the {{c1::Dependency Inversion Principle}}.
In pattern 1 Checkout holds `{{c1::Paypal processor;}}; in pattern 2 it holds {{c1::Paypal& processor;}}; in pattern 4 it holds {{c1::IPaymentProcessor& processor;}}`.
fields.Extra: By value = composition; by reference bound in the constructor = aggregation.

fields.Text: The principle of the lecture: couple to {{c1::abstractions}}, not {{c1::concretions}} - because the type you name in a member declaration is the type you are stuck with.
